summary: Open with a small bitcoin position of $250 and keep the other three quarters in cash, because bitcoin is in a falling trend and is resting on a long-term support line that may or may not hold.
thesis:
Bitcoin closed 11 November at $73,928 and was trading near $73,500 to $73,700 around the time of this decision. It is down about 16% from its September peak and roughly 7% over the past month. It sits below its 20-day average (about $78,100) and its 50-day average (about $81,400), and only about 1% above its 200-day average (about $73,100), which it briefly broke on Tuesday. By the plan's own test, bitcoin below its recent average and falling, this is a time to hold less.

The reasons behind the fall have not gone away. October US consumer prices rose 0.4% on the month, more than expected, and futures now put the chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase on 9 December at roughly 85% to 95%. Higher interest rates usually weigh on assets like crypto. US spot bitcoin funds have lost money on most days this month, about $1.3 billion in the first week alone, and the largest fund had seven straight days of withdrawals to 9 November. Sentiment gauges read fear (Fear and Greed index in the high 20s), and reports say small investors are not buying the dip.

There are two reasons not to sit entirely in cash. First, the account is measured against simply holding bitcoin, so owning none is itself a large bet. Second, the price is at a level where long-term buyers have often stepped in, the pace of fund withdrawals has slowed (from $412 million on Friday to $201 million on Monday), and fearful sentiment tends to come late in a decline rather than early. A quarter of the account in bitcoin keeps me in the game if the line holds and limits the damage if it does not.

I am not buying other coins. Ether, Solana and XRP have all fallen more than bitcoin over the past month (Solana about 19% and below its own 200-day average), ether funds are also seeing withdrawals, and none has a specific reason of its own that would justify the extra risk right now.

What I will do next: add to bitcoin, and consider ether, if bitcoin closes back above about $75,500 and then its 20-day average with fund flows turning positive. Hold at this size while it drifts between about $72,000 and $75,500. Cut the position if bitcoin posts daily closes clearly below about $72,000, which would mean the 200-day line has failed. This view is wrong if bitcoin rebounds sharply from here, in which case I will lag the benchmark and pay up to rejoin.
risks: If bitcoin bounces hard off its 200-day average, three quarters of the account in cash will fall behind the benchmark. If the line breaks, the $250 position loses money, though far less than a full holding would. The fill is at the 13 November open, which could differ noticeably from today's price. The averages and fund-flow figures come from news reports rather than my own calculation and may be slightly off. The Fed decision on 9 December and inflation data on 25 November could move prices sharply either way.
strategy_change: Plan moved to version 2. It now names the measures of trend (the 20-day, 50-day and 200-day averages of bitcoin's price) and sets rough exposure bands: about 0-30% invested when bitcoin is below both shorter averages, about 30-60% once it is back above the 20-day average, and up to fully invested when it is above both and rising. It also notes that the 35% limit per holding means matching bitcoin in an uptrend requires holding other coins, with ether as the default second holding.

orders.reason: Starter anchor position, about 25% of the account, at the 200-day average while the shorter trend is still down.

summary: Open the account three quarters invested: $300 in an S&P 500 fund, $300 in an equal-weight S&P 500 fund and $150 in a health care fund, keeping $250 in cash until Nvidia's results and the December interest rate decision are out of the way.
thesis:
This is the first trade. The account starts with $1,000 in cash and the plan says to stay mostly invested with a broad core.

The backdrop is mixed. The S&P 500 fund SPY ended 11 November at $759.81, about 4% above its 200-day average ($731) but just under its 50-day average ($765) and roughly flat over one and three months. Under that calm surface a lot has moved. Technology and chip stocks have fallen hard (XLK down 8.4% and the chip fund SMH down 10.2% over 20 trading days) while health care, banks, consumer staples and the average stock have risen (XLV up 8.6%, XLF up 7.5%, and the equal-weight fund RSP up 5.0% over the same 20 days). RSP is above its 20, 50 and 200-day averages; SPY and the Nasdaq fund QQQ are below their 50-day averages.

Three things are pushing in that direction. First, inflation: October consumer prices rose 0.4% against 0.3% expected, the 10-year Treasury yield is at about 5%, and markets put the chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase on 9 December at roughly 86% to 88%, with one Fed governor saying a larger increase should be considered. Higher rates hurt the most expensive stocks most. Second, the largest company in the index has a leadership crisis: Nvidia's board has opened an investigation into its chief executive and is reported to be weighing whether to remove him, the shares were down more than 5% before the open today, and its results are expected around 18 November. Third, the recovery in chip stocks this week has won back less than a third of what they lost since early October. Futures on the morning of 12 November pointed to the S&P 500 opening about 0.4% lower and the Nasdaq 100 about 0.8% lower.

What I am doing about it:

1. SPY, $300 (30%). The plain core. Proved wrong, and cut, if SPY ends a day below its 200-day average (about $731), which would say the long rise has broken.

2. RSP, $300 (30%). This fund holds the same 500 companies in equal amounts, so it has far less riding on Nvidia and the other giant technology companies than SPY does. It is the main way this account differs from the benchmark: a bet that the average company keeps doing better than the giants while rates rise and the AI trade is in doubt. Proved wrong if RSP ends a day below its 50-day average (about $215), or if over the next month it trails SPY by more than 3 percentage points while technology recovers above its own 50-day average. In either case I would move it into SPY.

3. XLV, $150 (15%). Health care has the strongest trend of any sector on the watchlist (up 11.3% in 60 days, above all three averages) and investors have been using it as shelter from the technology sell-off. It has already run a long way, 18% above its 200-day average, which is why this is half the size of the other two. Proved wrong if XLV falls more than 8% from the purchase price or ends a day below its 50-day average (about $174), or if a concrete change in US drug pricing or insurance policy undercuts the sector.

4. Cash, about $250 (25%). The plan says cash needs a reason and an end date. The reason: within four weeks there is a likely rate increase with a real chance of a larger one, a possible change of chief executive at the index's biggest company, and that company's results. Buying everything on one morning ahead of all three is not needed. The end date: the rest goes into the market no later than the first trading day after the Fed decision of 9 December, and sooner if Nvidia's results pass and SPY is back above its 50-day average. I am leaving this in plain cash because moving it into a Treasury bill fund and back would cost about as much in fees as the interest earned over four weeks.

I considered bank and consumer staples funds, which are also rising, but RSP already holds them and a first portfolio does not need more than three lines. I considered waiting a day because of the weak futures; a 0.4% lower open is a slightly better price, not a reason to stay out. Weekly jobless claims were due after this was written and are not reflected here.

This is the first decision of the month but there is no earlier month on the books, so there is no monthly review; the first is due at the start of December.
risks: If technology and chip stocks rebound sharply, for example on good Nvidia results or a quick settlement of its leadership question, SPY will beat this account because RSP, XLV and cash all hold less technology. Health care has risen a lot in a short time and could give back several percent quickly if the money sheltering there leaves. A rate increase larger than expected, or the 10-year yield moving well above 5%, would likely pull down everything held here, and smaller companies inside RSP are more sensitive to borrowing costs than the giants. Holding 25% in cash loses ground to the benchmark if the market simply rises from here. Prices are from the close of 11 November; the orders fill at today's open, which may differ.

orders.reason: Broad core holding; the long rise is intact with the price about 4% above its 200-day average.
Same 500 companies in equal amounts, so much less depends on Nvidia and giant technology stocks; above all its averages and leading SPY over the past month.
Strongest sector trend and a shelter from the technology sell-off; kept to half size because it has already risen a long way.

summary: No new orders today: bitcoin fell about 3% to around $71,500 to $72,000 and slipped under its 200-day average, so the account stays at the single $250 bitcoin purchase already on its way and keeps the rest in cash.
thesis:
Bitcoin's last price of 11 November was $73,928. During 12 November it fell to between roughly $71,200 and $72,000, its lowest since August, and was near $71,600 in the early evening UTC. That puts it below its 20-day average ($77,705), its 50-day average ($81,120) and now also about 2% below its 200-day average ($73,116), the long-term line it was resting on yesterday. Ether dipped under $2,000, and Solana, XRP and the other large coins fell 3% to 5%.

Several things hit on the same day. Nvidia said its chief executive had left with immediate effect and its shares fell about 13%, dragging down technology shares and crypto with them. The index provider MSCI said it will remove Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, from its main indices at the end of November, which forces index funds to sell that company's shares. US spot bitcoin funds lost about $300 million on 11 November, the fifth straight day of withdrawals and about $1.44 billion in total, and ether funds lost about $145 million. More than $650 million of borrowed bets on rising prices were forcibly closed. Behind all of it, October inflation was higher than expected and markets put the chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase on 9 December at about 90%. The supply of dollar-pegged stablecoins, a rough gauge of money waiting to buy crypto, has shrunk by about $14 billion in a month.

What I can and cannot do today. Yesterday's $250 bitcoin purchase has not been made yet: it is made at the first price of 13 November, and the rules do not allow an order to be withdrawn. A sell order sent today would be handled at that same moment, before the purchase, when there is nothing yet to sell, so it would simply be turned away. The real choice today is therefore whether to add, and the plan says no. With bitcoin below both shorter averages and now under the 200-day average, the plan calls for the bottom of its 0-30% range. The purchase on its way is about 25% of the account, already near the top of that range, so I am adding nothing, in bitcoin or anything else. One small comfort is that the purchase will be made roughly 3% cheaper than the price at which I decided on it.

No other coin earns a place. Every coin on the watch list is below its 20-day and 50-day averages, most have fallen further than bitcoin over the past month, and none has news of its own strong enough to outweigh that.

What happens next. Yesterday I said I would cut the position if bitcoin ended its days clearly below about $72,000. Today is ending right around that level, which is a warning but not yet a clear break. If 13 November also ends below about $72,000, I expect to sell at least half of the position in tomorrow's decision, and all of it if the price is heading toward the August low near $69,300. If instead bitcoin climbs back above its 200-day average near $73,100 and holds there, I keep the position, and I still need to see it above about $75,500 with money returning to the bitcoin funds before adding. Doing nothing today is wrong if this was a one-day panic and bitcoin snaps back sharply, in which case three quarters of the account in cash falls behind simply holding bitcoin.
risks: The $250 purchase goes ahead at the first price of 13 November into a falling market, and if the slide continues it will be showing a loss by the time I can sell, though a loss on a quarter of the account is far smaller than the loss on holding bitcoin outright. If the market rebounds hard, the cash will lag the benchmark. US producer price figures on 13 November and a Federal Reserve speech on 14 November could move prices sharply either way. Today's prices come from news reports published between about 14:30 and 18:30 UTC, not from the exchange itself, and the price at midnight UTC may differ.
